extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific, philosophical, and legal reasoning (readers learning the logic of induction and common fallacies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and avoiding the principal mistaken modes of generalization and inductive inference (confusing perception and inference, illicit universal generalizations, bad reductions, simple enumeration, causal-confusion, and false analogies). Intended to help form sound scientific and philosophical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inference from direct perception
rubrics_metrics.description: When mingling inference with reported facts, be aware which part of an assertion rests on immediate consciousness (indisputable) and which part on inference (questionable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always mark what is perception versus what is inferred. Examples: witnesses often mix impressions and conjectures with direct observation; untrained narrators describe impressions as facts. Cross-examiners must restrain witnesses from presenting inferences as perceptions. Be explicit about the epistemic status of each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat appearances as definitive evidence of their common-sense interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearances may be equally reconcilable with multiple theories; what one 'sees' need not be what is actually the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Copernican example: people 'saw' the sun rise/set but that appearance was compatible with different cosmologies. Avoid taking intuitive appearance as proof of an underlying reality without further analysis or theory-testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extending observed laws beyond the domain of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from phenomena observed on Earth or in the solar system to remote parts of the universe are not warranted by available experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of empirical scope: unobserved regions may operate under different laws. Refrain from assuming uniformity beyond adjacent or similar cases without causal justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal negatives (assertions of impossibility) cannot be established by experience alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-existence of a phenomenon, however uniformly observed to date, cannot justify concluding it is impossible; absence of observed causes only shows those causes haven't manifested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer impossibility from lack of observation. Only in cases governed by immutable laws (see exceptions) can impossibility be affirmed. Maintain epistemic humility about what causes may exist but remain undiscovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only number/extension laws and universal causality justify impossibility claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The only natural laws that can warrant asserting impossibility are (1) laws of number and extension (mathematical/structural constraints) and (2) the universal law of causality (no change if antecedents identical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish when an impossibility claim is supported by formal/mathematical necessity or by strict causal determinism versus when it is merely empirical absence. Be explicit which category a purported impossibility falls into.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid resolving radically different phenomena into a single element (illicit reductionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to reduce qualitatively distinct phenomena (e.g., sensation, colour, consciousness) to one fundamental element (motion, electricity, chemistry) is necessarily false when it pretends to eliminate the generic peculiarity of the phenomenon rather than merely identify conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's permissible to show physical conditions or necessary antecedents for a phenomenon, but not to claim that those conditions are a full explanation that removes the distinct nature of the phenomenon. Example: showing motions in the nervous system are conditions for sensation does not thereby explain the qualitative character ('the law of colour' remains distinct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple enumeration (enumeratio simplex) as a sufficient method of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by mere listing—'this A, that A, therefore every A'—is a crude and precarious method that concludes provisionally and risks contradiction by counter-instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper induction requires separation of nature by rejection/exclusion (eliminative methods), systematic comparison of instances, and attention to alternative explanations. Beware social maxims and stereotypes that arise from mere enumeration without elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate empirical (observed) laws with causal (explanatory) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations that express customary order are not equivalent to laws of cause and effect and should not be treated as ultimate causal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical summaries as provisional descriptions of observed regularities; seek underlying causes to elevate them to causal laws. Beware placing empirical laws on the same certainty footing as causal laws, especially in social and historical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware post hoc and cum hoc causal fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer causation merely from temporal succession (post hoc ergo propter hoc) or mere coexistence (cum hoc ergo propter hoc) of events without elimination of other antecedents or independent grounds for causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal claims need elimination of alternative antecedents and supportive evidence that the candidate cause has properties tending to produce the observed effect. Single instances of conjunction are weak verification; seek additional, independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false theoretical simplifications that attribute all phenomena to a single agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that one simple principle explains all instances of a class (e.g., all disease from one bodily condition) is a false theory when coexisting agents or causes are overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple coexisting causes and the complexity of phenomena. Historical medical and political examples show the danger of attributing effects to a single dominant cause without critical testing and elimination of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analogy as weak, inconclusive evidence unless causal connection is known
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument from analogy (inferring B in a case because it resembles a case that has B) supplies at best a small, non-assignable increase in probability; it is not a substitute for causal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogy only as a tentative presumption when direct proof is unavailable. Strengthen analogical inference by demonstrating a causal link between the shared property (A) and the inferred property (B); if such a causal link is shown, the inference becomes inductive, not merely analogical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overrate the probative force of analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy is often overvalued, especially by those with narrow imaginative range who perceive few analogies and hence overweight them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cognitive bias: more imaginative or better-informed thinkers will see many analogies that conflict and thus be less prone to overrating any single analogy. Seek corroboration beyond analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false analogies that infer similarity of one property from similarity of another when evidence disconnects them
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that resemblance in one respect implies resemblance in another is fallacious when there is no causal link and when evidence even suggests disconnection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the shared properties are materially connected to the inferred property. Examples of false analogies: parental government ≠ political despotism; body politic ≠ natural body aging; metropolis ≠ heart of organism in disease implications. Expose disanalogous relevant differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of sweeping empirical generalizations about human society
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations about human nature or social trends derived solely from a limited historical or cultural sample (e.g., assuming human nature is constant or that progress is universal) are empirical laws with narrow limits and may be false when causes differ across times/places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing about society, identify and analyze the specific causes producing observed changes; do not assume a single summary law (e.g., 'progress of species') without causal investigation. Limit claims to adjacent cases unless causal relations are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elimination and causal analysis to elevate empirical patterns to genuine laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn observed regularities into reliable predictive laws, ascertain the causes that produced the successive changes and determine circumstances that might check or reverse them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform investigations that trace determinate causes of observed phenomena and test how different combinations of causes affect outcomes. Predictions about future states require knowledge of causal mechanisms, not merely empirical series.
